text: Course 7 taught you how to build one integration well — REST Messages, Scripted REST APIs, IntegrationHub, and OAuth-based authentication for that integration. This lesson asks a different question: once an enterprise has dozens of integrations built by dozens of people, how do you make sure the next one doesn't quietly repeat the mistakes of the first ten?

A single integration can be built correctly and the enterprise can still be in trouble, because it was designed in isolation. Nobody necessarily knew another team built a similar integration months earlier. Nobody checked the authentication pattern the rest of the instance uses. An integration strategy is the enterprise deciding, deliberately, how integrations get designed, documented, and governed — so well-built and well-governed become the same outcome.

The concrete deliverable of that strategy is an integration inventory: a maintained record of every integration touching the instance, documenting the external system, direction, pattern, authentication method, and both a business owner and a technical owner. Without this record, knowing what's actually integrated with the instance means interviewing every team that's ever touched the platform — and the answer is usually still wrong.

A missing strategy causes three real, expensive problems. Duplicate integrations, where two teams independently connect to the same external system because neither could check an inventory. Inconsistent authentication, where some integrations use OAuth, others Basic Auth, and a few a hardcoded key nobody's rotated. And the worst one: nobody holding a complete picture of what depends on what, which turns outages and security reviews into guesswork.

An integration strategy turns course 7's technical best practices into enterprise-wide policy: every new integration gets an inventory entry before it ships, OAuth is the default unless there's a documented exception, and a named owner reviews new integrations against the existing inventory before they're built, not after. Next: choosing between request-response and event-driven integration at enterprise scale.
